wa_eldorado_peak_east_ridge.name: Eldorado Creek climbers' path to Inspiration Glacier high camp
wa_eldorado_peak_east_ridge.hours: 5-7 to high camp, 3-5 more to the summit
wa_eldorado_peak_east_ridge.notes:
Drive Cascade River Road from Marblemount roughly 20 miles to the Eldorado parking area at about 2,100 ft. The first ten miles are paved; the rest is gravel and washboard.

The path does not leave from the parking area. Walk back down the road about 90 feet and look for the log (historically a large single log, sometimes a clump of trees) spanning the Cascade River. The crossing shifts year to year and is slick when wet — a handline is worth carrying for a party that is not confident on a log. On the far bank walk perpendicular to the river roughly 100 feet to pick up the boot path.

The path climbs steeply and relentlessly through old-growth timber with no water, gaining about 1,500 ft before it breaks out into the boulder field. Follow cairns and flagging up the boulders, staying climber's right so you do not cross Eldorado Creek unnecessarily. The boulder field is universally described as the worst part of the trip, and worse on the way down with a heavy pack.

Above the boulders the ground eases into Eldorado Creek Basin (roughly 5,400-5,600 ft, about 3 miles and 3,300 ft from the car), a common first camp. To continue, climb onto the rocky ridge at about 6,100 ft and drop a few hundred feet on the far side into Roush Creek Basin (6,100-6,400 ft, running water). From Roush, broken talus and slabs lead onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier; rope up here. Moderate glacier slopes lead to high camp on the Eldorado-Inspiration saddle around 7,500-7,800 ft.

Overnight stays need a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit. Eldorado is a high-use cross-country zone; there is an advance lottery and reservations on Recreation.gov, but permits for the areas off Cascade River Road (Eldorado, Boston Basin, Cascade Pass) must be picked up in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.
wa_eldorado_peak_east_ridge.season: Jul-Sep, once the talus is bare
hazards: Cascade River log crossing — slick when wet, position shifts year to year
Boulder field is the crux of the walk, worse descending under a heavy pack
Crevasses on the Eldorado and Inspiration Glaciers, worsening as the day warms
Featureless flat glacier — whiteout navigation to The Gap
Exposed summit knife-edge; crevasses on the ridge crest itself
wa_eldorado_peak_east_ridge.baseFinding:
There is no rock start on this route — the climbing is the summit snow arete, and finding it means finding one gap on an otherwise featureless glacier.

From high camp on the Eldorado-Inspiration saddle the Inspiration Glacier runs away nearly flat to the west. Cross it aiming for the obvious low gap in Eldorado's lower East Ridge, universally called 'The Gap'. Once you have stepped through the gap you are on the East Ridge; before that you are still on flat glacier.

The confirmation underfoot is that the ground stops being flat and becomes a defined crest, with glacier falling away on both sides rather than one. From the gap, go a short way further up onto the snow until a distinct ramp leads leftward/rightward onto the ridge crest proper — parties consistently report a gentle ramp reaching the base of the knife edge from its far right side. That ramp, and the point where the crest narrows so that both sides drop, is the base of the climbing.

The common error is stopping short: the flat Inspiration is genuinely disorienting in cloud, parties describe an hour of whiteout walking to reach the gap, and parties drift too low into crevassed glacier instead of holding the line to the low point on the skyline. Take and hold a bearing from camp. Later in the season the crest melts out and parties move onto the steeper snow slope to the right of the bare ridge, where crevasses open — early season the same crest can be broad enough to skin.

Stay roped on the ridge. It is not a rock ridge you have escaped the glacier onto; the line travels back onto glacier and crevasses exist on the crest itself.

wa_eldorado_peak_east_ridge.name: Late-spring snow cover (skis or boots)
wa_eldorado_peak_east_ridge.notes:
In late spring the upper approach is continuous snow and the boulder field problem largely disappears, which is why many parties prefer this window. It does not make the whole approach snow: a late-May park report described the route as snow-free until just before Eldorado Basin was gained around 5,000 ft, with the boulder fields completely melted out — so expect a dry, steep forest climb first and snow only above.

Ski parties commonly carry ski boots and walk the forest section in approach or running shoes, switching over at snow line.

The trade is avalanche exposure. Large avalanches sweep parts of this route in winter and spring, and Cascade River Road itself can be buried by avalanche debris miles below the trailhead in a heavy year, adding road miles before you even start.
hazards: Avalanche paths across the approach and the road in spring
Snow-bridged creek channels in the lower basins — parties have punched through
Road may be closed or buried well below the trailhead
wa_eldorado_peak_east_ridge.baseFinding: Same gap in the lower East Ridge, but early season it is broader and more forgiving: the ridge is wide, sometimes wide enough to skin, and the knife edge that defines the route later in the summer may not have formed yet. Do not treat a wide, easy crest as evidence you are in the wrong place — the landmark is still The Gap, the low point on the ridge skyline reached by crossing the flat Inspiration.

wa_emerald_peak_west_route.name: North Fork Entiat Trail #1437 to the meadow camp
camps: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
Fox Camp, North Fork Entiat trail
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.notes: Drive the Entiat River Road and then the switchbacking forest-road spur to the North Fork Entiat Trailhead, and follow North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437 up-valley. Almost all of the distance to the peak is on trail. The usual staging point is the trail camp in the meadow below the summit around 6,700 ft, and the climb starts from the tread a short way north of it. The base-finding below is written for this trail camp side.
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.season: Mid-July into early October. Snow can hold in the gullies well into the season, and an axe is worth carrying early and mid-season.
hazards: Deep loose scree with a dug-in boot path; kicked rock runs onto parties below, so spread out and wear a helmet
Several gullies, correct one hidden until you round a buttress
Small summit area becomes exposed within a few paces of its centre
South point is a steeply inclined slab; a slip runs down the East Face
Nearby sub-summits are convincing and have been tagged by mistake
No water beyond the meadow
Remote, minimal cell coverage
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.baseFinding: The small boggy meadow where the trail turns sharply left is the departure. From the meadow camp, follow the tread north until it turns sharply left at a small boggy meadow around 6,900 ft — past that turn the trail carries on around the south shoulder of the neighbouring peak, which is not where you are going. Leave it there and climb north, or slightly east of due north, over open ground almost to the ridge crest between the two peaks. Just before the crest, look for a scree and talus slope leading up and to the right to a notch on the northwest ridge. Take that about halfway, then cut right and south into the adjacent gully, and climb it to the depression between the two summits. Expect to see several gullies on the way in and not the one you want: it stays hidden until you round a buttress, and cairns only start marking the way once you are past that corner. The true summit is the north point, to the left of the depression as you arrive. Do not use a register to settle which point you are on — parties have found none on either.

wa_emerald_peak_west_route.name: Emerald Park trail from Lucerne

bivy.name: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
bivy.notes: The high camp for the crest traverse, about a mile and a half beyond Fox Camp on the Pyramid trail, in the basin that separates Emerald Peak from Saska Peak. This is where a party stages to link Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain in a single push over Milham Pass at about 6,663 ft, which is the classic way to do these four and much the most efficient. From the basin you climb to the upper shelf just below the ridge between Emerald and Saska and pick up the broad gully to the summit. Cardinal is the highest of the group and the furthest, and it is the one that turns a two-day plan into three. The setting is superb and the ground is loose — expect scree and blocky scrambling rather than clean rock, and expect the descents to take longer than the ascents. Season is short at this height in a heavy year, realistically mid-July to early October, and the reason to come late is the larch and the reason not to is the water. Weigh that honestly: an August party that finds the tarns dry has a long, hot walk back down to fix it. Weather moves in from the west with little warning here and the basin is fully exposed.
bivy.water: Snowmelt tarns and rivulets in the basin, and these are the crux of the whole plan. They are dependable in early and mid summer, unreliable by mid-August, and in a dry year they are gone entirely by late August, at which point the nearest certain water is back down at Fox Camp. Do not commit to a high camp here in late season without either confirming water or carrying it up. Milham Pass itself has none.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue, party limit of twelve. Camp on durable ground and well back from the tarns. No campfires — forest-wide restrictions aside, there is no fuel at this elevation and the ground is fragile. The trails in have been closed by the Little Giant Fire closure; check the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest for current closures before you go.
bivy.capacity: A small number of tent-sized spots on benches and moraine in the upper basin; two or three parties at most, and less if you want flat ground

wa_emerald_peak_west_route.notes: Take the boat up Lake Chelan to Lucerne, follow the Domke Lake trail to the Emerald Park trail, and climb up Emerald Park to Milham Pass, which drops into the basin between Emerald and Saska. A boat-dependent alternative to the Entiat side, and the natural choice when coming from Lake Chelan. It reaches the peak from Emerald Park via Trail #1230 out of the lakeshore settlement. Where this line joins the climbing is unclear.
hazards: Approach trails affected by a wildfire closure; check status before going
Boat-dependent access from Lake Chelan
Rockfall and loose rock in the erosion-carved west gully
Exposure on the south summit slab toward the East Face
Basin tarns unreliable by mid-August; camp fully exposed to weather from the west
Remote, minimal cell coverage

wa_energizer_bunny.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, to the left side of the south face
camps: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
wa_energizer_bunny.notes:
The shared Core Enchantments approach: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, the boulder field at the south end, and Aasgard Pass — 2,000 ft of loose scree in 1.25 miles, hazardous under snow into early July.

From the pass, cross-country north past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn, roughly 7.5 to 8 miles and 4,600 ft one way from the trailhead.

Five pitches, about 450 ft: a burly and somewhat dirty roof pitch straight off the deck, an exposed corner to a good ledge, a short aid section through steep ground, a fingery crack between two features, and then the final corner crack shared with the neighbouring line to finish.

Because it joins that neighbour near the top, it shares its descent: a single full-length rappel on the north side and about thirty minutes of scrambling back round to the base.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: 2,000 ft of loose scree, with hidden creek and moat under early-season snow
Burly, dirty roof pitch immediately off the ground
Short aid section at mid-height adds rope-management complexity
Dirt and lichen on the lower pitches from little traffic
Shared north-side rappel anchors rebuilt and relocated over the years
Afternoon weather arrives unseen from behind the peak
Long approach
wa_energizer_bunny.baseFinding:
The roof at ground level is the marker, and it is the only one you need. This route starts underneath a large roof formation at the very base — climbing it is the first pitch, straight off the deck. No other line at this end of the peak starts under a roof. Standing under a big overhang means you are here.

It is on the left side of the south face, just left of Solid Gold. If you have turned the corner onto the west side of the peak, you have gone too far left.

Mid-route confirmation: there is a pair of rock features partway up that the route is named for, with a steep fingery crack running between them. If you never pass between two distinct features, you are not on this line.

And the top: this route joins its neighbour's final corner crack, so the last pitch is shared and the summit is not reached directly — you finish on the West Ridge. That shared finish is also why the rappel descent is the same one.

wa_energizer_bunny.name: Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments

bivy.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
bivy.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.
bivy.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
bivy.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

bivy.name: Gnome Tarn
bivy.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. Getting there means leaving the main basin route and scrambling up from around Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass on a faint, easily lost path over granite. It is exposed and high, so a night here can be considerably colder and windier than the lakes below. The camping is on rock, which is both the right surface to use and the reason a level spot takes some hunting.
bivy.water: The tarn itself, though it is small and can drop low or silty late in a dry season; the lakes below are the fallback
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded

wa_energizer_bunny.notes: The longer, more gradual way in from Icicle Creek Road: the Snow Lakes trail climbs past Nada and Snow lakes to Lake Vivianne, about ten miles with well over 5,000 ft of gain, looking straight at Prusik's south face. From Vivianne continue past the upper lakes to Prusik Pass and round onto the west face. It avoids the loose grind of Aasgard Pass at the cost of roughly two more miles and a thousand more feet.
hazards: Long approach, about ten miles and well over 5,000 ft of gain to Lake Vivianne, then past the upper lakes to Prusik Pass
Burly, dirty roof pitch immediately off the ground
Short aid section at mid-height adds rope-management complexity
Dirt and lichen on the lower pitches from little traffic
Shared north-side rappel anchors rebuilt and relocated over the years
Afternoon thunderstorms

wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.name: Basalt Ridge crest to Fifth of July Pass
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.notes: This is the shorter alternative to the Entiat River approach. From the Basalt Pass trailhead, climb to the pass — the small stream in the gully below it is the last water, and there is none at all beyond — then follow the ridge north. The trail bypasses the first high point about 300 ft below it, and beyond the trail fork the tread fades into slick pumice. Continue north past the neighbouring tower's saddle, then through a col around 7,480 ft on the next peak's southwest ridge, dropping through a scree gully into the basin west of it. Hop the massive boulders in that basin, cross a small larch meadow, and regain the ridge. The peak can also be reached from the Entiat River side by way of Myrtle Lake, the Larch Lakes and Cow Creek Pass — that is the line the main approach and waypoints describe; the marks below are written for this Basalt Ridge side.
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.season: Mid-July through early October, and popular in early autumn for the larch.
hazards: No water beyond the stream in the gully below Basalt Pass
Slick pumice where the ridge trail fades out
Scree gully descent off the col and a 500 ft loss into the boulder basin that must be regained
Loose rock and tree debris on the south ridge
Long open ridge fully exposed to afternoon weather
Lingering snow on north-facing terrain into early July
Remote, unreliable cell coverage
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.baseFinding: A larch forest and then Fifth of July Pass is the gateway to the south ridge. After the boulder basin and the small larch meadow put you back on the ridge, the ground drops gradually and you walk through a larch forest immediately before arriving at Fifth of July Pass — that named saddle is where the south ridge begins, and the larch immediately below it is the confirmation. From the pass the south ridge is straightforward, with tree debris to avoid, and a short traverse along a long, broken ridgetop reaches the high point. The negative marker is the neighbouring tower: Devils Smoke Stack is a separate and harder summit with a sheer north side, climbed by steep gullies on its south with two tall steps of choss, and it lies on the far side of the intervening peak. You cannot arrive at one thinking it is the other without crossing that peak in between — so if the ground ahead rears into a tower with sheer cliffs on its north and no walkable line, you are back at the Smoke Stack rather than on this mountain's long broken crest.

wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.name: Entiat River and Larch Lakes
camps: Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.notes: From the trailhead at the end of the Entiat River road, follow the Entiat River trail up the valley and climb the side trail to the Larch Lakes meadows. From a camp between the lakes the summit is a modest day out along the ridge. Longer than the Basalt Ridge line, but on maintained trail with water, so it suits multi-day trips and loops.
hazards: Burned and downed timber on the lower Entiat River and Cow Creek Meadows trails
Footbridge gone at the river crossing near the 4-mile mark
Open unmarked cross-country routefinding above Cow Creek Meadows
Loose talus and scree on the summit slopes
Sun exposure and limited water on the steep final trail mile into the meadows
Lingering snow on north-facing terrain into early July
Remote, unreliable cell coverage

wa_flora_mountain_southwest_slope.name: Devore Creek Trail from Bird Creek Camp over the Enigma saddle
camps: Purple Point and Harlequin — the landing camps, and the boat that decides the trip
wa_flora_mountain_southwest_slope.notes: Come up the lake by passenger ferry or floatplane, ride the shuttle up the valley road to the bridge, cross it and follow the road past the camp and the airstrip to pick up the river trail. Follow that mostly flat trail southeast to the signed Devore Creek Trail junction, then climb steeply through rock bluffs and open forest into the wilderness and traverse brushy, dry hillside to Bird Creek Camp — the only designated camp in that stretch of trail, sitting about fifty yards before the creek crossing, with room for about three tents and a cook area. From camp the peak is a long day of its own; it does not combine with the neighbouring summit above the same camp, and every account allows a full day for each.
wa_flora_mountain_southwest_slope.season: Midsummer into early autumn, and tied to the boat and shuttle timetable at both ends.
hazards: Off-trail navigation with no tread through the woods; two ways to end up in the wrong basin
600 ft descent off the divide into the creek that must be reclimbed on return
Talus degrades from solid boulders to fist-size rock moving underfoot
Loose rubbly gneiss throughout
Access only by Stehekin ferry or floatplane and shuttle; long evacuation
Lingering snow and cornices early season; whiteout navigation
Rockfall from parties above
wa_flora_mountain_southwest_slope.baseFinding: Two elevations tell you you are in the wrong place, and both are worth memorising. Leave the trail at about 5,000 ft, cross the creek and bear east-southeast; if you have climbed to 5,200 ft you have gone too far along the trail and risk dropping into the wrong basin when you turn off. Then, if you find yourself heading cross-country into a narrow basin as early as 6,200 ft, you are too far south — contour northward at once, round the corner below the steeper ground, and get into the next basin over. The correct basin leads to a divide at about 7,460 ft on the south ridge of the neighbouring peak, reached up an increasingly steep and unstable talus slope to an obvious saddle on climber's left, the rock starting as large solid boulders and degrading into loose softball- and football-sized stuff. From the divide, descend about 600 ft off its east side toward the creek, contouring around at roughly 6,800 ft to avoid steeper ground, then aim for the high southwest basin, from which a simple talus scramble reaches the top. The true summit is the south end of the massif; the north point is about a hundred feet lower.

wa_flora_mountain_southwest_slope.name: Holden Village over Tenmile Pass
wa_flora_mountain_southwest_slope.notes: From Holden, climb to Tenmile Pass, descend the shoulder into upper Riddle Creek, then traverse northeast into the Castle Creek basin to join the standard line around 6,500 ft. Longer and more involved than Devore Creek; mostly used to combine Flora with Riddle Peak, or by parties exiting to Holden after climbing from Stehekin.
hazards: Long, involved route over Tenmile Pass and down into upper Riddle Creek before traversing to Castle Creek basin
Loose rubbly gneiss and shifting talus on the summit slopes
Remote wilderness; long evacuation if injured
Lingering snow and cornices early season; whiteout navigation
Rockfall from parties above

wa_forbidden_peak_west_ridge.name: South face couloir to the West Ridge notch
wa_forbidden_peak_west_ridge.notes: From the Boston Basin high camp, traverse up and east across talus and the remains of the Quien Sabe Glacier toward Forbidden's south face. Where the glacier is melted out, a class 3 rock spur on climber's right is usually faster and drier than staying on snow; where it is snow-covered or crevassed, rope up. The couloir itself runs about 500 ft and steepens to 40–50° near the top, which is where crampons and an axe stop being optional. Reaching the notch is roughly 2,000 ft above camp.
wa_forbidden_peak_west_ridge.season: Jun–early Aug, while it still holds snow
hazards: A moat where the snow pulls back from the rock guards the top of the couloir. Expect a short steep step or a band of loose rock to get over it, and expect it to be worse the later in the season you go.
Rockfall once the sun reaches the couloir — parties above are the usual source, so it pays to be off it early.
40–50° snow near the top, on ground where a slip does not stop on its own.
wa_forbidden_peak_west_ridge.baseFinding: The notch is the gap in the crest at the foot of the West Ridge proper, and the couloir below it is the obvious continuous snow line splitting the left-hand edge of the south face. Navigate to the notch, not to the first gully you reach — several lines start off the same snowfield and only this one tops out at the crest. You are at the base of the climbing when you step through the notch onto the ridge crest; from there the route to the summit runs to climber's right.

wa_forbidden_peak_west_ridge.name: Cat Scratch gullies (late season, once the couloir has melted out)
wa_forbidden_peak_west_ridge.notes: When the couloir has gone to loose talus and scree, the usual line moves off the snow onto the rock gully system immediately west — climber's left — of it. Roughly the first 200 ft is class 4, easing to grassy class 3 for the last 200 ft to the notch. It is loose the whole way, and it is slower than it looks on the approach.
hazards: Loose rock from bottom to top. Keep the party out of one another's fall line rather than spread across the gully.
The parallel gullies are easy to confuse, and committing to the wrong one puts you on the ridge away from the notch with loose ground to traverse back.
wa_forbidden_peak_west_ridge.baseFinding: Cat Scratch is not the snow couloir, and that mix-up is the usual reason parties lose time here: it is the parallel rock gully system just west (climber's left) of the couloir, and it tops out at the same notch. Several parallel gullies in that system look alike from below — the correct one finishes at the notch itself rather than on the ridge either side of it, so pick your line by where it ends on the skyline, not by which entrance looks easiest from the basin.

wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.name: White Chuck River and Kennedy Ridge to the 7,200 ft camp

bivy.name: Kennedy Ridge high camp
bivy.notes: Planned camp and the standard high camp for the route, on an open ridge crest of snow and pumice reached by a climbers' path leaving the PCT. Pumice takes stakes poorly — bring something to anchor to snow or rock. Fully open to weather in every direction, with a straight view up at the mountain. Everything above this is snow and glacier, so this is the last comfortable ground.
bivy.water: snowmelt; last running water is the creek crossings on the approach below
bivy.capacity: several parties spread along the ridge crest

bivy.name: Vista-Kennedy saddle
bivy.notes: Planned intermediate camp on the saddle where the route rounds Kennedy Peak and steps onto the Kennedy Glacier. Bivy sites exist here and it is used to shorten summit day, but it puts you above the last easy ground with nothing to hide behind.

bivy.name: 8,800 ft saddle at the foot of Frostbite Ridge
bivy.notes: Planned high camp and the last dependable bivy before the crater. Rocky ridge ground at the top of the Kennedy Glacier's loose moraine, and it is exposed enough to cost you the night — one party was battered by wind here until dawn and concluded afterwards that a platform cut into the lee snow would have been the right call. Site low and downwind of the crest, not on it.
bivy.water: snowmelt only; a documented trick is bagging snow on sun-warmed rock
bivy.capacity: a small tent or two on rock, better platforms cut into lee snow

bivy.name: Ledge near 9,900 ft below the ridge crux
bivy.notes: Emergency only. A spot has been reported at about this height below the steep sections, and the party who found it said plainly they would not count on it being there. No shelter, extreme exposure, and immediately below the loose rock of the Rabbit Ears where warm dry conditions turn the ground overhead into a rockfall hazard. Use it if you must, never plan on it.

wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.notes:
The White Chuck River Trail was destroyed by a 2003 flood and has no road or trail access, so this approach is no longer usable; reach Kennedy Ridge from White Pass on the PCT instead. The old line ran from the White Chuck River trailhead at about 2,300 ft. Follow the White Chuck River Trail (FST 643) about six miles to the Kennedy Ridge Trail (FST 639) junction, then Kennedy Ridge Trail about a mile and three quarters to the PCT.

Head north on the PCT past the Glacier Creek crossing, which is your water, to an unmarked climbers' path leaving the trail on Glacier Ridge about two thirds of a mile beyond the creek. That path climbs snow and pumice to the standard high camp near 7,200 ft on the Kennedy Ridge shoulder.
hazards: Road access on the White Chuck side has long-running problems and the river trail is gone, so this way in is likely unusable
Unmarked climbers' path leaving the PCT
Loose moraine and boulders low on the Kennedy Glacier
Crevasses on the Ptarmigan, Vista and Kennedy glaciers
Very loose rock around the Rabbit Ears, worst in warm dry conditions
Steep snow/ice to ~50 degrees, cornices on the ridge
Committing ridge with no easy retreat; remote
wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.baseFinding:
The high camp at about 7,200 ft on snow and pumice is the staging point, not the route. From there the approach continues across the upper south-west slopes of the Ptarmigan Glacier just below the ridgeline to about 8,000 ft, rounding Kennedy Peak to a saddle at 8,000 ft between the Vista and Kennedy Glaciers, then up the Kennedy Glacier — loose moraine and boulders low down — to a saddle at about 8,800 ft. That saddle is where Frostbite Ridge proper begins, and it is the last bivy site before the crater.

The critical navigation warning is about the Rabbit Ears. They are the route's famous feature, a pair of eroded lava pinnacles, and they are not visible until you are immediately below them, slightly east of the ridge crest. Do not try to navigate toward them from a distance and do not conclude you are off route because you cannot see them — get to the 8,800 ft saddle and follow the crest, and they will appear.

Above the Ears the ridge steepens into alpine ice, reported anywhere from a single short step to a couple of hundred feet, before the crater rim.

wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.name: Suiattle River Road and the PCT via Milk Creek

bivy.name: Kennedy Ridge high camp
bivy.notes: Planned camp and the standard high camp for the route, on an open ridge crest of snow and pumice reached by a climbers' path leaving the PCT. Pumice takes stakes poorly — bring something to anchor to snow or rock. Fully open to weather in every direction, with a straight view up at the mountain. Everything above this is snow and glacier, so this is the last comfortable ground.
bivy.water: snowmelt; last running water is the creek crossings on the approach below
bivy.capacity: several parties spread along the ridge crest

bivy.name: Vista-Kennedy saddle
bivy.notes: Planned intermediate camp on the saddle where the route rounds Kennedy Peak and steps onto the Kennedy Glacier. Bivy sites exist here and it is used to shorten summit day, but it puts you above the last easy ground with nothing to hide behind.

bivy.name: 8,800 ft saddle at the foot of Frostbite Ridge
bivy.notes: Planned high camp and the last dependable bivy before the crater. Rocky ridge ground at the top of the Kennedy Glacier's loose moraine, and it is exposed enough to cost you the night — one party was battered by wind here until dawn and concluded afterwards that a platform cut into the lee snow would have been the right call. Site low and downwind of the crest, not on it.
bivy.water: snowmelt only; a documented trick is bagging snow on sun-warmed rock
bivy.capacity: a small tent or two on rock, better platforms cut into lee snow

bivy.name: Ledge near 9,900 ft below the ridge crux
bivy.notes: Emergency only. A spot has been reported at about this height below the steep sections, and the party who found it said plainly they would not count on it being there. No shelter, extreme exposure, and immediately below the loose rock of the Rabbit Ears where warm dry conditions turn the ground overhead into a rockfall hazard. Use it if you must, never plan on it.

wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.notes:
Drive the Suiattle River Road (FR 26) from Darrington to its end at Sulphur Creek Campground. Follow the Suiattle River trail about seven miles to the bridge over the river, then the PCT southbound about nine miles to a camp in the East Fork Milk Creek basin at about 5,600 ft. From there continue up the ridge on snow and pumice to the same standard high camp near 7,200 ft.

The Suiattle River Road has a long history of flood damage and multi-year closures, so its status is worth confirming rather than assuming.
hazards: Repeated flood damage and long closures on the Suiattle River Road
Very long PCT approach day
Crevasses on the Ptarmigan, Vista and Kennedy glaciers
Very loose rock around the Rabbit Ears, worst in warm dry conditions
Steep snow/ice to ~50 degrees, cornices on the ridge
Committing ridge with no easy retreat; remote
wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.baseFinding: Identical above the 7,200 ft camp: traverse the upper south-west Ptarmigan slopes to about 8,000 ft, round Kennedy Peak to the 8,000 ft saddle between the Vista and Kennedy glaciers, up the Kennedy to the 8,800 ft saddle where the ridge begins. Remember that the Rabbit Ears stay hidden until you are directly beneath them slightly east of the crest.

wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.name: North Fork Sauk to White Pass, then north
camps: 8,800 ft saddle at the foot of Frostbite Ridge
Ledge near 9,900 ft below the ridge crux
wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.notes: Some parties use the North Fork Sauk trail to White Pass — about nine miles and 5,900 ft — and then make a long traverse north on or near the PCT to the same Kennedy Ridge camp area. It is a twenty-mile-plus approach day and is chosen when the other two roads are out.
hazards: Twenty-mile-plus approach day
Crevasses on the Ptarmigan, Vista and Kennedy glaciers
Very loose rock around the Rabbit Ears, worst in warm dry conditions
Steep snow/ice to ~50 degrees, cornices on the ridge
Possibly unstable old rappel slings at the Rabbit Ears
Committing ridge with no easy retreat; remote
wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.baseFinding: Same as the other variations: the 8,800 ft saddle above the Kennedy Glacier is where the ridge starts, and the Rabbit Ears do not become visible until you are immediately below them.

wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.name: White Chuck River and Kennedy Ridge to the Glacier Creek camps

bivy.name: Kennedy Ridge and the Glacier Creek camps, Suiattle side
bivy.notes: This is the base for Glacier Peak's Kennedy Glacier and for the Frostbite Ridge line above it, and it is also reached from the Suiattle side. The walk in from there is long even when the road is open — the Suiattle River trail runs about seven miles to the river bridge and the crest trail then carries you south toward Kennedy Ridge, so this is a full day before the climbing camp is even in sight. Kennedy Creek has no bridge and will not get one; the standard tactic is to camp short of it and cross in the morning when the flow is at its lowest, using whatever logs are in place rather than wading the main channel. Above the forest the route climbs the ridge and the glacier toward the saddle between the Kennedy and Vista glaciers at around 8,000 feet, where bivouac sites exist for parties willing to sleep on snow and rock with no shelter and no clean water. With the road washed out the trailhead is normally reachable on foot or by bike from the closure point, which adds roughly eighteen miles each way to an approach that was already the longest on the mountain, and a fire closure has also shut the upper Suiattle River Road, the Suiattle River Trail and the PCT from Mica Lake north; check with the Darrington Ranger District before planning this way in.
bivy.water: Glacier Creek and Kennedy Creek are both right there and both silty with glacial flour — let it settle or filter accordingly. Higher on the ridge water disappears entirely by late season and has to be carried or melted.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Suiattle road end. Stove only above the forest. Check the road order before driving: the Suiattle River road washed out about four and a half miles in during the December 2025 storms and is closed to vehicles at that point under a closure order that runs into 2028 unless lifted sooner, with the campgrounds and trailheads up the road closed.
bivy.capacity: Forested sites in ones and twos scattered along the crest trail near the creek crossings, plus rougher bivouac ground higher on the ridge; nothing organised, and no single site takes a large party

wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.notes:
The historic line starts at the White Chuck River Trailhead at the end of FR-23 and follows Trail #643 about four miles, then Kennedy Ridge Trail #639 for 1.7 miles to the Pacific Crest Trail near 5,000 ft. Turn north on the PCT and follow it about two miles to the Glacier Creek crossing, where there are established camps with reliable water near 5,300 ft. Four to five hours is the usual pack-in.

FR-23 has been closed from milepost 3.7 to its end, so the reliably open option in recent seasons has been the North Fork Sauk Trail and the PCT over Red Pass to the same Glacier Creek camps. That is a much longer walk to the same place, and it changes nothing above camp.

From the Glacier Creek camp a climbers' trail runs up a gully to the crest of Kennedy Ridge. Everything above is glacier, and the character of the day is set by how well you read the upper glacier rather than by any technical difficulty — the headwall at the top is about 40 degrees and short, while the crevasse field below it is the part parties spend hours on.
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.season: Roughly Jun-Aug, and it is one of the shorter windows on the mountain — the upper Kennedy is a small, steep glacier that opens into a maze of 5-15 ft crevasses as the season runs on
hazards: Walk in may be far longer than the mileage because the road is closed at milepost 3.7
8,200 ft of gain from the trailhead
Upper glacier is a maze of 5-15 ft crevasses needing slow routefinding
Seracs on climber's left under the Kennedy Peak wall
Hugging the left wall trades crevasses for rockfall from Kennedy Peak
Bergschrund at the glacier head, possibly only one bridge
Remote; long, difficult evacuation
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.baseFinding:
The start of the climb is below you, not above you, and that is the whole test. From the Glacier Creek camp the climbers' trail climbs a gully to the crest of Kennedy Ridge — and then you go down off the far side, to climber's right, to the foot of the Kennedy Glacier. A party that tops the ridge and keeps climbing has left the route. If you have not lost height since the ridge crest, you have not reached the base.

Arrival: the foot of the glacier, where ridge ground runs out into ice. Rope up there. On the lower glacier keep right; on the upper glacier take the centre. That right-then-centre sequence is worth memorising before you leave camp, because the upper Kennedy is a maze and there is nothing to sight on inside it.

The discriminator against Frostbite Ridge, which shares this mountain flank and this camp: Frostbite rounds Kennedy Peak to the saddle between the Vista and Kennedy glaciers at about 8,000 ft, climbs the Kennedy to a saddle at about 8,800 ft, and then leaves the ice for the ridge. This route never leaves the ice. If you are standing on a saddle looking for a rock crest to follow, you are on Frostbite. If you are still roped on glacier at 9,500 ft heading for a bergschrund, you are on this one.

The top end, and it is a real decision point: the bergschrund sits at the head of the glacier. Reach it by climbing left to the top of a snow dome and looking for a bridge from there — do not walk the schrund's length hunting for a gap at its lowest point. Above it the headwall runs about 40 degrees; stay left of, but close to, the prominent rock outcrops, and that puts you on the crater rim.

What hugging the left wall costs: parties commonly move under the Kennedy Peak wall on climber's left to simplify the crevasse problem. It works, and it buys the simplification with rockfall and serac exposure. That is a trade to make deliberately, not one to drift into.

wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.name: North Fork Sauk and the crest trail north
camps: Kennedy Ridge and the Glacier Creek camps, Suiattle side
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.notes: Walk the North Fork Sauk trail up the valley and climb to the crest trail near White Pass, then follow it north past Red Pass, across the White Chuck basin and on toward Kennedy Creek, descending to the bench below the glacier. Long, with real elevation loss on the way, but this is how most parties now reach the Kennedy side.
hazards: Long approach with real elevation loss on the way to the bench below the glacier
Upper glacier is a maze of 5-15 ft crevasses needing slow routefinding
Seracs on climber's left under the Kennedy Peak wall
Hugging the left wall trades crevasses for rockfall from Kennedy Peak
Bergschrund at the glacier head, possibly only one bridge
Remote; long, difficult evacuation

wa_glacier_peak_sitkum_glacier.name: North Fork Sauk Trail and the PCT over Red Pass
wa_glacier_peak_sitkum_glacier.notes: The way in since the White Chuck side closed. North Fork Sauk Trail #649 runs up the valley through old growth to Mackinaw Shelter and then switchbacks steeply to the Pacific Crest Trail at about 5,950 ft, roughly eight to nine miles from the trailhead. Turn north on the PCT, cross Red Pass a mile or two on, and descend into the upper White Chuck valley, following the PCT down it for roughly seven to nine miles past the old White Chuck River Trail junction to Sitkum Creek. It is much longer than the old approach, and the climb back over Red Pass comes on the way out.
hazards: very long approach on the PCT with substantial gain and loss
no signed junction for the climbers' path
wa_glacier_peak_sitkum_glacier.baseFinding: The route above is unchanged: the marker is Boulder Basin — trees giving way to heather and rock benches with running water at roughly 5,500 to 6,000 ft — and then snowfields onto the toe of the Sitkum above it. Coming down the valley on the PCT the risk is walking past the start of the climbers' path, so mark the old White Chuck River Trail junction and Sitkum Creek on the map before you set out rather than expecting signage.

wa_glacier_peak_sitkum_glacier.name: White Chuck River Trail #643 (closed since the 2003 flood)
wa_glacier_peak_sitkum_glacier.notes:
This was the standard way up Glacier Peak until the October 2003 flood. The White Chuck Road (FR 23) is now closed to vehicles at milepost 3.7 and the trail has been listed as inaccessible since the flood, so this is kept as a record of the old line rather than as a way in.

From the trailhead at about 2,350 ft the trail runs upstream through old growth, crossing Pumice, Glacier and Kennedy Creeks — reliable water, but high with snowmelt in early summer. At about five and a half miles is the old Kennedy Hot Springs area at around 3,300 ft, still a popular campsite; the pool, lodge and guard station were destroyed by the 2003 flood and never rebuilt, so there is no usable hot pool there.

Another mile and a half brings you to Sitkum Creek and the PCT junction at about 3,850 ft. Turn north on the PCT for about half a mile to a forested camp near 4,100 ft.
hazards: road closed to vehicles at milepost 3.7 and trail listed as inaccessible
creek fords running high with early-summer snowmelt
steep unmaintained climbers' path with no signage leaving the PCT
crevasses on the Sitkum
wa_glacier_peak_sitkum_glacier.baseFinding:
The path that leaves the PCT for Boulder Basin is unsigned and steeper than anything before it — climbers describe it as more of a fisherman's track than a trail. The test is direction, not appearance: the correct path goes straight up the forested ridge. Anything that contours is the PCT or a game trail.

You know you have arrived at the top of it when the trees break: Boulder Basin at roughly 5,500 to 6,000 ft is heather and rock benches with running water, and it is the standard high camp. If you are still in continuous forest, you are below it, however long the climb has felt.

From camp the route ascends snowfields onto the toe of the Sitkum. Rope up at the point the snowfield stops being a slope you can see the bottom of and becomes continuous glacier — there is no rock landmark for this, so the transition is judged on the ground rather than found.

wa_golden_age.name: Up the gully to its own ledge
wa_golden_age.notes: From the pullout near milepost 166, hike the gully below the wall for about an hour and follow a narrow ledge back right to the start, a prominent left-arching wide corner. The direct way, and the most practical when the gully is in shape.
hazards: Loose talus and an exposed easy-fifth step in the approach gully
Rockfall in the gully, especially with parties above or after rain
Full-day south-facing sun and heat in summer
Loose and deteriorating rock on pitches 1, 2 and 6
Loose chockstones in the first corner above the start
Highway gated shut through winter, so the wall is unreachable by car for months

wa_golden_age.name: Via the centre route's lower pitches
wa_golden_age.notes: You can scramble on up the gully to this climb's own ledge, but many parties add pitches instead: do the usual gully approach from the pullout near milepost 166 to the wall's upper ledge, then climb the lower pitches of the centre eleven-pitch line to the shared midway ledge system and traverse left from there. Rack for the pitches you are climbing to get there as well as for this route.
wa_golden_age.season: Summer, once the wall has dried; the pitches used to reach it are the same ones that seep into early summer in wet years.
hazards: Retreat from the lower pitches means reversing or rappelling a different route
Loose, deteriorating rock on the lowest pitches and again high on the line
Not all belays are rigged for rappel; find the stations before you need them
Rockfall onto parties on the route you climbed in on
Rockfall in the approach gully and exposed easy-fifth step
Full-day south-facing sun; lower pitches seep into early summer in wet years
wa_golden_age.baseFinding: You are looking for a two-bolt anchor sitting on the midway ledge, and the trees are what place it: the anchor is on the ledge below a stand of trees, not level with them and not above them. Traverse left along the ledge until the trees are above you and the two bolts are at your feet. Confirm it from the rock: the first pitch off this anchor is a technical corner with loose chockstones at its hardest moves, so if what rises from your anchor is a clean face or a slab you are at the wrong station. Negative markers: if the anchor you have clipped is one of the bolted rappel stations belonging to the route you just climbed, you have not traversed at all; if the trees are still off to your left, you have not traversed far enough.

wa_golden_age.name: Via the right-hand cave route's lower pitches
wa_golden_age.notes: The same idea from the other side: climb the lower pitches of the right-hand cave line off the upper ledge to reach the shared midway ledge system, then traverse left. This is the longer leftward traverse of the two, so allow for it.
wa_golden_age.season: Summer, once the wall has dried.
hazards: Escape means rappelling a neighbouring line
Loose, deteriorating rock low and high on the route
Not all belays are rigged for rappel; plan the descent before leaving the ledge
Long leftward traverse on a ledge with loose material
Seepage on the lower pitches into early summer in wet years
Full-day south-facing sun; loose talus in the approach gully
wa_golden_age.baseFinding: From the midway ledge, traverse left — further than from the centre line — until you find the two-bolt anchor set on the ledge directly below a stand of trees. The trees are the test: below them, not beside them. The first pitch above the anchor is a technical corner holding loose chockstones at the crux, which distinguishes it from the clean faces either side. Negative markers: if you are still passing bolted rappel stations that belong to the route you climbed up, keep traversing; if you have reached ground where the ledge system ends and the wall closes down, you have gone past it.

wa_gray_wolf_ridge_se_slopes.name: Lower Maynard Burn Trail #816 over Baldy and along the crest
wa_gray_wolf_ridge_se_slopes.notes:
There is no roadside access to this ridge; the drive only gets you to the trailhead at the end of FR-2860-120, off FR-2870 / Lost Mountain Road, itself off Palo Alto Road south of US-101 near Sequim. Road-end parking at a dirt berm, about 3,300 ft, Northwest Forest Pass required.

Lower Maynard Burn Trail #816 leaves the berm on an old roadbed and crosses Mueller Creek almost immediately — the last easy reliable water for a long stretch, so fill up. The trail narrows to single-track around 0.3 mile and then turns relentlessly steep, gaining roughly 3,000 ft in a little over two miles of fall-line tread with essentially no switchbacks, in places barely a boot-width across eroded crumbly ravine crossings and slopes of packed dirt and shattered shale. It is a climber's path, not a graded trail.

At about 2.7 miles and 6,200 ft it tops out on the saddle between Tyler Peak and Baldy, where a short steep side path drops off the crest to a snowmelt spring — the last dependable water on the route.
wa_gray_wolf_ridge_se_slopes.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. North-facing gullies on the last stretch hold steep snow into July
hazards: Sudden fast-moving whiteouts and lightning on an open above-treeline ridge with miles of exposure
Loose shale and scree with occasional exposed steps along the crest
Lingering steep snowfields in north-facing gullies into July, warranting an ice axe
No reliable water once past the Baldy saddle spring
Long unmarked ridge navigation with route-finding around gendarmes and false summits
The Gray Wolf River bridge on the old Gray Wolf Trail route is out — do not plan to come in that way without a hazardous ford
Bear canister required within Olympic National Park
wa_gray_wolf_ridge_se_slopes.baseFinding:
The climb begins where the tread ends, and the arrival test is the saddle between Tyler Peak and Baldy. You know you are there because the trail stops going up in a line and the ground opens on both sides — navigation shifts from following tread to reading a ridge. There is also a signed Olympic National Park boundary marker in a saddle on this stretch and a spring path dropping off the crest. From here on you are on the crest and the crest is the route.

The test that actually matters on this route is at the far end, and it is a false summit with a name and a number: point 7076. From below, 7076 reads as the summit. It is not. The true summit of Gray Wolf is 7,218 ft and it lies further north along the crest and is higher. So the fog rule is simple: after Baldy you drop about 600 ft, climb back up over a prominent bump, and that bump is not the top. Keep going north over the last of the talus, detouring briefly round the occasional gendarme, and finish with a short Class 2-3 scramble on loose rock. If you turned round on the first big bump past Baldy, you turned round on 7076.

Second test, on the way to 7076 itself: the crest gets steeper and broken approaching it. The published avoidance is to traverse west at about 6,500 ft and then swing back to gain 7076 by its northwest aspect, and to stay in the basin below and right of the broken rock ridge until you can gain the saddle between the twin summits — 7076 has twin tops with snowfields between them. There is no trail at these decision points, which is why they are written down.

Third test, earlier: Point 6537 is a rocky gendarme and false summit below Baldy, normally skirted on its south side rather than climbed over. If you are scrambling straight over a tower before you have reached Baldy, you have taken the crest too literally.

Honest limit: long stretches of this crest are unmarked and off-trail and the whole thing is above treeline. Carry a map or GPS; the ridge is the handrail but the summit identification is not obvious by eye.

wa_gray_wolf_ridge_se_slopes.name: Royal Basin and the east face, for a traverse rather than an out-and-back
wa_gray_wolf_ridge_se_slopes.notes:
The other end of the same ridge, and the reason to know it is that it turns this route into a traverse instead of a there-and-back over Baldy twice. From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, the Royal Basin Trail leads to Royal Lake and Upper Royal Basin. From the ridge, the east face drops roughly 3,000 ft to intersect the Royal Basin Trail.

It is steep, loose and only lightly travelled: packed dirt and shattered shale, brushy notches, and picking through timber looking for blazes and cairns. Some parties scree-ski the looser upper sections rather than rope up at all. It is not a bolted or standardised line — where parties do rope down a short cliffy step, anchors are improvised from trees or natural rock horns.

Most commonly this is used as the exit after climbing from Maynard Burn, closing a loop out Royal Basin or back over the ridge.
hazards: Steep, loose, lightly travelled ground with no established line and improvised anchors if roped
Roughly 3,000 ft of descent or ascent on packed dirt and shattered shale
Brushy notches and timber navigation looking for blazes and cairns
Committing: once on the east face there is no easy return to the crest
Every ridge-crest hazard above, in a longer day
wa_gray_wolf_ridge_se_slopes.baseFinding: Used as an approach, the arrival test is gaining the crest — and this side has no marker sequence for doing it. Parties describe finding blazes and cairns through timber rather than following a line. Treat it as navigation, not route-following. The summit tests once on the crest are the same and they are the valuable part: Point 7076 is a false summit. Coming from the Royal Basin side you meet the true 7,218 ft summit from the north-east rather than from the south, so the trap runs the other way — the bump you must not stop on lies south of the true summit on this approach. Fix which side of you 7076 should be before you commit to the crest in cloud. Honest limit and a recommendation: this variant is known as a descent far more than as an ascent, and there is no fixed, repeatable rappel count for the cliffy step — expect at most one or two short rappels well under 60 m if you choose to rope, and expect most parties to downclimb or scree-ski instead. Confirm current conditions before relying on it either way.

wa_gunn_peak_southeast_route.name: Barclay Creek climbers' path — summer line
wa_gunn_peak_southeast_route.notes: From the Barclay Lake trailhead, do not take the maintained lake trail. Walk back down the access road about a quarter mile and pick up the old deactivated spur road — parties who know it often park at the spur's gated start instead of the main lot. Follow the old roadbed a hundred or two hundred yards to a fire-pit clearing, turn right, and pick up the unmarked but well-trodden climbers' path. It drops to the creek and crosses on a log jam or by rock-hopping near the downstream tip of a small mid-channel island; this crossing is the main early-season hazard. On the far bank the path swings west, then north, and starts climbing in earnest through sustained tight switchbacks in second-growth timber. Two decision points follow. Around thirty-six to thirty-eight hundred feet the path forks near a band of exposed rock — stay right and do not scramble the outcrop straight ahead, which is a known trap; the correct line keeps traversing climber's-left beneath a cliff band. Then around forty-four hundred feet the summer line bends left up a brushy weakness in the cliff band rather than continuing up the couloir, which holds snow late. Huckleberry and heather meadows lead to the saddle at about fifty-four hundred feet, the last reliable water.
wa_gunn_peak_southeast_route.season: June to September. Early June parties meet significant lingering snow and heavy brush; late July through August is typically the clearest.
hazards: Steep brush — alder, devil's club and salmonberry — on the lower approach
Log-jam crossing of the creek is slick and runs high in spring
The fork near the exposed rock band around thirty-six to thirty-eight hundred feet is a known route-finding trap; the outcrop ahead is not the way
Loose rock on the talus fan and at the ramp
No reliable water above the creek and the waterfall ravine in late summer
Cairns thin out badly above treeline and the boot path fades in the talus; route-finding rather than difficulty is the main hazard here
Multiple search-and-rescue incidents have occurred on this peak
wa_gunn_peak_southeast_route.baseFinding: From the saddle, drop about a hundred feet off the crest to skirt a cliff band and boulder-hop up the talus fan toward the upper tree benches directly below the peak's south face. The base of the technical ground is the top of that fan — and the feature you are looking for cannot be seen from below. A ramp cuts up the face from the top of the talus and only appears once you are underneath it, which is exactly why parties overshoot by continuing up the rockslide. The unmistakable test is the single step at the ramp's foot: a boulder with two options off it, a left-hand line past a chockstone that takes a steep low-fifth move, and a right-hand line, steeper and more exposed but on solid holds, which is what most parties take. If there is no boulder with a two-way step above it, you are not at the ramp. Negative marker: if you are still grinding up loose rockslide with no ramp cutting off to either side, you have gone past the entry — the ramp is entered from the talus, not from the top of it. Higher up, the next landmark is a keyhole notch through the ridge to the north side; if you have not passed the ramp step you will not reach it.

wa_gunn_peak_southeast_route.name: Tailgunner couloir — snow-season line
wa_gunn_peak_southeast_route.notes: The same start — the spur road, the fire-pit clearing, the creek crossing at the island, and the switchbacks up through the timber. The difference comes at about forty-four hundred feet: instead of bending left into the brushy weakness in the cliff band, the snow-season line continues directly up the couloir to the saddle. This same couloir is a documented wrong turn in summer and an avalanche path, so it is only reasonable when it is a continuous snow climb and conditions have been assessed.
wa_gunn_peak_southeast_route.season: Late spring, while the couloir holds continuous consolidated snow. Once it starts melting out it becomes the wrong answer and the summer line through the brushy weakness is correct.
hazards: Avalanche hazard — this couloir is an active path and holds snow late
Snow conditions vary hour to hour on it; assess before committing
Everything the summer line carries below the cliff band, including the brushy lower approach and the creek crossing at higher spring flow
The ramp above is harder to protect and downclimb when wet or holding snow, and it is the one place on this peak where parties commonly rappel
wa_gunn_peak_southeast_route.baseFinding: The couloir tops out at the same saddle as the summer line, so the base of the climbing is identical: drop about a hundred feet off the crest to skirt the cliff band, then boulder-hop up the talus fan to the upper tree benches below the south face. The ramp at the top of the fan is invisible until you are under it; identify it by the boulder at its foot with a two-way step above — a left-hand chockstone move at low fifth, or a steeper, more exposed line on good holds to the right. Negative marker: if you are still on snow when you expect to be on talus, you have carried on above the saddle into the wrong basin; the couloir delivers you to a saddle, and the talus fan starts on the far side of it.
